title: Early life stages of Northeastern Pacific fishes exhibit uncoupled spatial and phenological variability in response to environmental change
content:
Abstract
In response to changing ocean conditions, marine fishes may shift where they are (geography) and/or when they are present (phenology) during environmentally-sensitive life stages, such as spawning. We compiled larval fish density data, a proxy for spawning, from 1995–2018 across six long-term ichthyoplankton sampling programs between the Baja California peninsula and the Gulf of Alaska. This is the first time that these datasets have been jointly analyzed, allowing for assessment of spatiotemporal distribution shifts across many species’ entire range. Spatiotemporal variability and trends were examined for 16 fish species from three types of adult habitats. We applied a model selection process followed by an analysis of five seasonal and geographic spatiotemporal metrics. Most species were best described by a “base” model that did not include seasonal or geographic shifts over the 1995–2018 time frame, or a model that allowed for changes in seasonal variance. Further, across all species, the magnitudes of seasonal and geographic variance were not correlated. Roughly half of species showed distributional shifts toward the northwest over the course of the study timeframe, while phenological shifts were much less common, which may be a reflection of the lack of long-term linear trends among environmental covariates evaluated. Using 10 life history characteristics, we found the strongest predictors of spatiotemporal variability to be the groundfish adult habitat category (negatively correlated with seasonal variance), and maximum lifespan (negatively correlated with all geographic metrics). The results of this study improve our ability to determine the adaptive capacity of commercially and ecologically important fishes to changing or variable ocean conditions.
